q-336882.name: Question 1
q-336882.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+y(t)-5 \\ {y}^{′}(t)={y}^{2}(t)+x(t)-3\end{aligned}
$$

Given the system of differential equations, select the correct options below. The Jacobian determinant of the system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[2,\text{ }1]^{T}$ is given as

$$
J(2,1)={{field-1}}.
$$

At this point, the system is 
{{field-2}}
at ${x}^{∗}.$
q-336882.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+y-5 \\ {y}^{2}+x-3\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y-5)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+y-5)=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+x-3)=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+x-3)=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}2x & 1 \\ 1 & 2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(2,1) & =|\begin{aligned}2(2) & 1 \\ 1 & 2(1)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =4\cdot 2-1\cdot 1 \\  & =7 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\text{almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

q-334949.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ {y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x))=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}2x & -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$

$$

The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}2x & 2y \\ 2x & -2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

$$

$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

q-335103.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ {y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y))=\pi x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1)=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-1)=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) & \pi x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) & 2y\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & \pi (0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\ -\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & 2(0)\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

q-334933.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}-{y}^{2}+1-{e}^{x} \\ -{x}^{2}+1-{e}^{y}\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{y}^{2}+1-{e}^{x})=-{e}^{x},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{y}^{2}+1-{e}^{x})=-2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}+1-{e}^{y})=-2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}+1-{e}^{y})=-{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}-{e}^{x} & -2y \\ -2x & -{e}^{y}\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}-{e}^{0} & -2(0) \\ -2(0) & -{e}^{0}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)-0\cdot 0 \\  & =1 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\text{almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

${u}^{′}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
q-336902.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3x+2y-1 \\ {x}^{2}+y-4x+4\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3x+2y-1)=2x+3,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3x+2y-1)=-2y+2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y-4x+4)=2x-4,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+y-4x+4)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x+3 & -2y+2 \\ 2x-4 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(1)+3 & -2(-1)+2 \\ 2(1)-4 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y+1\end{aligned}].
$$
